{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=computational+models+of+path-dependent+preference+formation+in+RL+agents&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"The successor representation in high-risk drinking and alcohol-related contexts.\", \"abstract\": \"The successor representation (SR) is a reinforcement learning strategy which has been suggested to underlie nuanced forms of habitual behavior, rendering it a candidate mechanism for mental health conditions thought to involve habitual control, such as addiction. However, paradigms used to assess habits in humans cannot detect SR use. Together with the fact that they are usually conducted in disorder-irrelevant contexts, this may explain why the evidence for a hypothesized shift from goal-directed to habitual behavior in addiction is inconsistent. Here, we tested whether individuals with high-risk (n = 260) compared to low-risk drinking behavior (n = 260) rely more on SR or a rigid goal-based dimension-reduced SR variant (redSR), particularly in alcohol-related contexts. An online multi-stage decision-making task performed in either a virtual bar or apartment context allowed us to dissociate (red)SR from model-based and model-free learning strategies by testing how well participants adapted their choices to different types of distal changes in the environment. Findings suggest that a particular type of SR, namely a (reduced) random-policy SR-like strategy, contributes to human behavior, but that high-risk drinkers do not differ from low-risk drinkers in their use of this strategy. Instead, both groups seem to rely less on what is likely a (reduced) random-policy SR strategy in alcohol-related contexts - and instead more on model-free control. Results suggest that the use of an adaptive, resource-efficient decision-making strategy is selectively downregulated in substance-related contexts. This study highlights the importance of considering contextual modulation and nuanced decision strategies in understanding habitual and goal-directed behavior in mental health conditions such as addiction.\", \"doi\": \"10.1371/journal.pcbi.1014873\", \"pmid\": \"42905773\", \"pmcid\": \"PMC13716319\", \"source\": \"MED\", \"fullTextUrlList\": {\"fullTextUrl\": [{\"availability\": \"…

{"url": "https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=computational+models+of+curiosity+and+problem+selection+in+autonomous+agents&format=json&resultType=core&pageSize=4", "scope": "Europe PMC search metadata, abstracts and full-text links; discovery only", "excerpt": "[{\"title\": \"Adaptive Digital Marketing: A Systematic Review of Bio-Inspired Reinforcement Learning, Multi-Agent Systems, and Agentic AI for Intelligent Optimisation.\", \"abstract\": \"

Background

Digital marketing increasingly functions as a complex adaptive system characterised by non-stationary environments, strategic interaction, and multi-agent competition. Programmatic advertising exemplifies this complexity, where decisions must be made in real time under uncertainty. Under such conditions, traditional static optimisation methods often fail to deliver robust performance. This review synthesises bio-inspired computational approaches, reinforcement learning (RL), multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) to develop an integrated theoretical perspective on adaptive optimisation in digital marketing.

Methods

Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we conducted a systematic search of peer-reviewed research across six databases: Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ACM Digital Library, SpringerLink, ScienceDirect, and arXiv, supplemented by manual reference checking. Each computational paradigm is explicitly grounded in foundational biological literature, including work on evolution, foraging, swarm intelligence, and immune cognition. Reinforcement learning supports adaptive decision-making through mechanisms closely aligned with operant conditioning and foraging behaviour. Multi-agent reinforcement learning extends these principles to interactive marketing ecosystems via decentralised coordination and swarm-based learning. Agentic AI further advances adaptive capability by introducing goal-directed reasoning, memory, and higher-level decision orchestration. Contributions: The review identifies persistent fragmentation across marketing sub-domains and a lack of formal mathematical grounding for widely used bio-inspired analogies. To address these gaps, the study proposes a multi-layer bio-inspired framework and outlines a structured research agenda to guide the development of autonomous digital marketing systems.\", \"doi\": \"10.3390/biom…

Harshit Bisht1 Vinay Kumar1 Kevin Maik Jablonka4,5,6
Mausam1,2,∗ N. M. Anoop Krishnan1,3,∗
Abstract
A growing body of work pursues AI scientists capable of end-to-end autonomous
scientific discovery. This position paper argues that although they already function
as co-scientists,agentic AI scientists are not built for autonomous scientific
discovery. We identify the following challenges in building and deploying au-
tonomous AI scientists: (1) Problem selection is influenced by the McNamara
fallacy; (2) Agents are built on large language models (LLMs) whose training
corpora omit tacit procedural and failure knowledge of laboratory practice; (3)
Preference optimisation during post-training compresses output diversity toward
consensus; and (4) Most scientific benchmarks measure single-turn prediction
accuracy and lack feedback from physical experiments back to the computational
model. These challenges are not just questions of scale and scaffolding; they require
revisiting fundamental design choices. To build truly autonomous AI scientists,
we recommend scientific simulations as verifiers for training, a persistent, mutable
epistemic state that carries beliefs and shifting objectives across an investigation,
the establishment of a centralized preregistration repository for all AI-generated
hypotheses, and application driven by scientific need rather than tool affordance.

Title:

Abstract:
A growing body of work pursues AI scientists capable of end-to-end autonomous scientific discovery. This position paper argues that although they already function as co-scientists, agentic AI scientists are not built for autonomous scientific discovery. We identify the following challenges in building and deploying autonomous AI scientists: (1) Problem selection is influenced by the McNamara fallacy; (2) Agents are built on large language models (LLMs) whose training corpora omit tacit procedural and failure knowledge of laboratory practice; (3) Preference optimisation during post-training compresses output diversity toward consensus; and (4) Most scientific benchmarks measure single-turn prediction accuracy and lack feedback from physical experiments back to the computational model. These challenges are not just questions of scale and scaffolding; they require revisiting fundamental design choices. To build truly autonomous AI scientists, we recommend scientific simulations as verifiers for training, a persistent, mutable epistemic state that carries beliefs and shifting objectives across an investigation, the establishment of a centralized preregistration repository for all AI-generated hypotheses, and application driven by scientific need rather than tool affordance.
